criteria.description: Correctly identifies value iteration uses the exact model, Q-learning a single noisy sample.
Correctly explains the additional requirements (decreasing step size, infinite visitation) needed for stochastic convergence.

solutions.fullSolution: Value iteration applies the exact Bellman update using the true model P,R at every state-action pair. Q-learning sees a single sampled transition and uses a noisy one-sample target. Its convergence proof needs a Robbins-Monro decreasing step size and every state-action pair visited infinitely often, on top of the same contraction argument.

criteria.description: Correctly describes UCT's continuous, graduated bonus and why it's preferred for large state spaces.

solutions.fullSolution: R-max: a binary switch, any pair visited fewer than m times gets the max possible reward assigned outright. UCT: a continuous, shrinking bonus proportional to relative under-visitation. Both encode optimism under uncertainty, but UCT's graduated form degrades more gracefully, suited to the huge state spaces MCTS is applied to.

criteria.description: Correctly identifies the linearity-of-expectation requirement for the Bellman recursion.
Correctly explains nonlinear U breaks this, requiring more than a scalar value function.

solutions.fullSolution: The Bellman recursion relies on expectation distributing over the sum of rewards. Nonlinear U breaks this (E{U(sum)} != U(head)+gamma*E{U(tail)} in general), so a scalar expected-utility value function is no longer sufficient for future decisions; risk-sensitive RL needs to track more of the return distribution.

criteria.description: Correctly computes both policies have equal expected value (10).
Correctly explains why a concave U prefers the guaranteed option via Jensen's inequality.

solutions.fullSolution: Policy B's expected value: 0.5*100+0.5*(-80)=10, equal to Policy A. Risk-neutral Q-learning tracks only expected return, so sees them as identical. A concave U satisfies U(E{X}) > E{U(X)} for random X (Jensen's inequality), so the guaranteed outcome's utility beats the risky bet's average utility, a distinction risk-neutral value functions can't express.
